title: The Byzantine churches
hook: Ukrainian, Melkite, Ruthenian, Romanian and more pray in the Byzantine tradition

segments.voice: Yesterday, sui iuris: of its own law, a family of churches inside one Church. Your line was one church, many churches.

Watch the hand. The thumb and the first two fingers press together at the tips. The last two fold down into the palm. Then the hand goes to the forehead, to the chest, to the right shoulder, and then the left. A Latin Catholic touches the left shoulder first. Three fingers joined, they say, for the Trinity; two folded, for the two natures of Christ, God and man. It's a small thing, a sign of the cross going the other way. And that hand belongs to a Catholic, praying in a tradition with long habits of its own.
screen: `THREE FINGERS JOINED, TWO FOLDED.` → `RIGHT SHOULDER, THEN LEFT.` → `A CATHOLIC HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Byzantine comes from Byzantium, the old name of the city later called Constantinople. The way of worship that grew up there, its liturgy, chant, icons and calendar of feasts, carried the city's name with it, and the Catechism lists the Byzantine among the Church's great liturgical traditions. Second, the churches. Several Eastern Catholic churches pray in this tradition, each its own church sui iuris: Ukrainian Greek Catholics; Melkites, whose home is in Syria, Lebanon and the Holy Land, and who pray in Arabic and Greek; Ruthenians, from the Carpathian mountains; Romanian Greek Catholics; and others. Different languages, different histories, the same shape of prayer. Third, the neighbors. The Byzantine Catholic liturgy is, for the most part, the liturgy of the Orthodox churches: the same prayers, the same icons, often the same music. The difference isn't in the incense; it's in communion. Byzantine Catholics are in full communion with the bishop of Rome, and name the pope in their prayers. They stand close to their Orthodox neighbors and close to Rome at the same time, and that place in between hasn't always been an easy one to hold. Fourth, the open door. The Church's law says a Catholic keeps the Sunday obligation by attending Mass in any Catholic rite. So a Latin Catholic can walk into a Byzantine Catholic church on Sunday, stand through a liturgy in another shape, receive communion from a spoon, and be welcome. Same Church. Different room.
screen: `BYZANTIUM: A CITY, THEN A TRADITION.` · `UKRAINIAN, MELKITE, RUTHENIAN, ROMANIAN.` · `CLOSE TO THE ORTHODOX, IN COMMUNION.` · `ANY CATHOLIC IS WELCOME ON SUNDAY.` · then, large: `EAST IN COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: If you like, make the sign of the cross their way, three fingers joined, two folded, forehead, chest, right shoulder, then left, and notice your hand doing something familiar a new way. Then hold them in mind: Ukrainians, Melkites, Ruthenians, Romanians, at home and far from home. If you pray, use a prayer sung in their liturgy, Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us; if not, simply hold them with good will.
The Byzantine churches. Eastern Catholic churches praying in the tradition of Constantinople, sharing worship with the Orthodox, in communion with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: east in communion. Close to the Orthodox, and one with Rome. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Byzantine Catholics celebrate the Divine Liturgy, sung throughout, with icons and incense; they make the sign of the cross from the right shoulder to the left, and Latin Catholics may attend and receive communion there.

chat.says: I'm Roman Catholic. Can I go to a Byzantine Catholic liturgy on Sunday?
options: Yes. Mass in any Catholic rite keeps the Sunday obligation, and you'd be welcome in the same Church.
No. Latin Catholics need a bishop's permission first, since it's really an Orthodox service.
Yes, but it won't count for Sunday, since only the Latin Mass keeps the obligation.

notes: Week-end look-back is in the carry (days 1352–1358).
The meaning given for the Byzantine finger position (three joined for the Trinity, two folded for the two natures of Christ) is the usual explanation; confirm.
'Melkites, whose home is in Syria, Lebanon and the Holy Land, and who pray in Arabic and Greek'; 'Ruthenians, from the Carpathian mountains': confirm.

'That place in between hasn't always been an easy one to hold' is deliberately general (it touches tensions with Orthodox churches and suppression of some Greek Catholic churches); confirm it is fair to Orthodox readers.

Canon 1248 §1 paraphrased: the obligation is satisfied by assisting at Mass celebrated anywhere in a Catholic rite. Confirm that 'receive communion from a spoon, and be fully at home' is acceptable for a Latin Catholic visitor.
The Trisagion is given in a common English form without quotation marks (translations vary), cited as paraphrase.
